t: Nothing in this title shall be construed as repealing any portion of section 7 of the District of Columbia Appropriation Act for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1903, approved July 1, 1902, as amended.

fable.w: This is a savings clause that only preserves an earlier appropriation act provision from implied repeal. It sets up no consultation, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue involving anyone outside the federal government. No reading of it brings an outside party into a federal decision.
fable.s: Nothing in this title shall be construed as repealing any portion of section 7 of the District of Columbia Appropriation Act

qwen_block.w: This section is a savings clause that preserves the legal effect of a previous statute. It does not establish any process for consultation, coordination, or input from outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) into a federal decision. It merely defines the scope of the current title's interaction with existing law.
qwen_block.s: Nothing in this title shall be construed as repealing any portion of section 7 of the District of Columbia Appropriation Act for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1903, approved July 1, 1902, as amended.

opus.w: This is a savings clause: it says the title does not repeal section 7 of a 1902 District of Columbia appropriation act. It sets up no consultation, hearing, comment period, advisory body, or right to sue. Reading in participation would mean guessing at what the referenced provision contains, and the text itself doesn't show any outside party taking part in a federal decision.
opus.b: This is a savings clause. It only keeps an earlier appropriations provision in force. Someone might be tempted to guess that the preserved section 7 involves some outside-party process, but nothing in the text shown here involves any party outside the federal government in a federal decision. So the answer is No.
